title: Mimamsa (ritual as meaning)
hook: a lullaby nobody remembers writing, and a school that says the Veda was never written by anyone

segments.voice: Yesterday Mimamsa answered a puzzle: the rite is over, the fruit comes later, and apurva carries it, like a letter in the bag. What did you send without tracking it? Day one thousand one hundred ninety, the end of a week.

A father hums a lullaby over a crib. His own mother sang it to him. Ask who wrote it, and he shrugs. Nobody wrote it. It was just always sung. Of course, somebody, somewhere, must have made it up first. We just lost the name. Mimamsa makes a much bolder claim about the Veda. Not that its author was forgotten. That it never had one. Today, to close the week, we hear why a school so focused on doing would care so much about who spoke the words.
screen: `A LULLABY OVER A CRIB.` → `NOBODY WROTE IT.` → `OR NOBODY EVER DID?`

segments.voice: Start with what Mimamsa needs. All week, its whole method has rested on one thing: dharma is known through the Veda's words, and nothing else can see it. So the words had better be reliable. If a person wrote them, a person could be wrong. Jaimini's answer comes in his fifth sutra. The bond between a word and its meaning, he says, is original. In Mimamsa's reading, nobody invented it. It's simply there. And so the Veda's instruction is a true means of knowing dharma, one that doesn't depend on anything else. Later Mimamsa thinkers spell out the consequence. The Veda is apaurusheya, not made by any person. It's heard and handed down, but never composed. Jaimini even meets an objection head on. Parts of the Veda are called after people, by names that sound like authors. Those names, he answers, come from the ones who taught and recited those parts, not from anyone who made them up. Here's why it matters to a school about ritual. If no one authored the words, then no one's mood, interest or mistake is hiding in them. The instruction can be trusted fully, and done fully. That's the week we've walked. Yoga set Ishvara at the top of the chain of teachers, and showed how traces wear a path. Mimamsa opened with the desire to know dharma, heard it in injunction, followed it through apurva, and today rests it on words with no author at all. Other schools hold other views of where the Veda comes from, and the tradition keeps all of them in the conversation.
screen: `THE WORDS MUST BE RELIABLE.` · `WORD AND MEANING, ORIGINAL.` · `NOT MADE BY ANY PERSON.` · `NAMES FROM TEACHERS, NOT AUTHORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to what was handed down for two minutes. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one line you were given, not one you made up. A blessing, a verse, a saying from home, a song. Let it play once, slowly, in your mind. Don't analyze it. Just notice it arriving, the way it always has, in the same words. Then rest in the quiet after it. If you pray, you can let that line be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Mimamsa. The school that holds the bond of word and meaning to be original, and the Veda to be apaurusheya, not made by any person.

Your line: Mimamsa, ritual as meaning. Today, when you say a line you were taught, a greeting, a grace, a blessing, say it once with full attention, exactly as it was handed to you. Day one thousand one hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Mimamsa holds that the bond between word and meaning is original and that the Veda is apaurusheya, not authored by any person, which is why its injunctions can be trusted as the means of knowing dharma.

fork.setup: an objector says: parts of the Veda carry people's names, so people must have written them. you're Jaimini. how do you answer?
options: the names come from those who taught those parts
those parts were added later and don't count
fork.reveal: Jaimini says the names come from teaching and reciting, not from authorship, so the Veda stays apaurusheya.

original.note: Sanskrit: not made by any person; Mimamsa's term for the Veda.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old text with no author just has a forgotten author.
what it means: Mimamsa says the Veda is apaurusheya, never authored, resting on an original bond of word and meaning.
what a scholar hears: Mimamsa Sutra 1.1.5 on the original bond of word and meaning, and the sutras that answer the objection from the names on Vedic recensions.

sources.ref: Mimamsa Sutras 1.1.5 (the relation of word and meaning is original; hence instruction is the means of knowing dharma, and it is independent)
Mimamsa Sutras 1.1.27–1.1.32 (the objection from names of Vedic recensions; names from expounding)

notes: The term apaurusheya is attributed to 'later Mimamsa thinkers', not to Jaimini; confirm.
Cut on purpose: a line that classical Mimamsa denies even divine authorship (true of the school, but not in the cited sutras).
Confirm the sutra range for the objection from names (Kathaka and others) and the reply that the names come from expounding (akhya pravacanat, 1.1.30).
Week-end day: the teach closes with a look back over 1184–1189.
'Other schools hold other views of where the Veda comes from' is general and unranked; check fairness.
